sub: An untested command doesn't cost you a failed unit test — it costs the university a drone. This module is the gate everything else in this course passes through.

title: One Bad Command Is All It Takes
desc: A drone has no undo, no rollback, no restore-from-backup

items: A crashed Mini 4 Pro is dead hardware and real money — the university paid for it once, and won't be happy paying twice
A flyaway is worse than a crash: the drone simply leaves and never comes back, and so does the course equipment
On a backend, a bad deploy is rolled back in minutes — a drone in a wall stays in the wall

rows: Climb velocity set with no ceiling and no stop condition — indoors it grinds into the ceiling; outdoors it climbs until the link drops and the drone is gone
Meters confused with m/s or with seconds of loop time — a wrong tick-rate assumption turns 2 m into 7 m, straight into a wall, the projector, or a person

items: Untested code never gets props. Not yours, not Claude's — no exceptions, not even for "trivial" one-liners. Especially not for those.

title: AI-Generated Flight Code: Compiles, Looks Right, Flies Wrong
desc: Claude writes Kotlin that reads clean and builds green — the drone doesn't know that

body.card: Why AI code is uniquely risky here
items: LLM-generated code fails plausibly: it compiles, reads clean, and a quick review nods it through
On a backend, a wrong unit is a failed test — on a drone the bug has propellers; the error budget is the distance to the nearest wall
Virtual stick has no "fly 2 m" command — only velocity × time at ≥ 5 Hz. Every distance is an implicit calculation the AI can silently get wrong

body.card: The trap: letting the same AI check itself
items: If the same AI writes the code and the tests, both inherit the same wrong assumption — the tests go green and the drone still hits the wall
A generated test that asserts distance == velocity * ticks proves nothing if the tick rate in the test is the same wrong guess as in the code
That is why this course demands a manual recheck of every test — you are the independent verifier the AI cannot be

title: Test Harness First, Flight Later
desc: Before any generated command flies: write the tests — then recheck the tests by hand

items: 1. Test framework first — unit tests for every distance / velocity / duration calculation before the flight code exists
2. Recheck the tests manually — read every assertion yourself and confirm the expected values against the SDK docs, not against the generated code
3. enableSimulator — fly the mission virtually and watch the telemetry: did it move 2.0 m, or 7?
4. Only then a real flight — indoors, propeller guards on, the SAFETY rules from the Lab module apply every single time
Every motion command has an explicit bound: max altitude, max distance, hard timeout
Units are visible in the code — distanceMeters, speedMetersPerSecond, durationMs — so a mix-up fails to read, not just to fly
The abort path is testable without the aircraft: the deadman timeout fires, virtual stick disables, the mission stops

title: The Gate: No Green, No Props
desc: This checklist applies to every flight, every time — there is no 'just a quick test'

items: ☐ Tests exist for every motion calculation — written before the flight code
☐ Every test manually reviewed against the SDK docs by a human
☐ Mission flown in enableSimulator — telemetry matches the intended distances
☐ Bounds, timeout and abort path verified
☐ Only then: props on, guards on, fly
This is verification independence (DO-178C, Module 4) at lab scale: the verifier must not be the author — and right now, the author is Claude
Module 11's Karate applies the same discipline to your backend: the telemetry pipeline gets tests before it gets traffic
Aviation learned this the expensive way — you get to learn it the cheap way
